narratives.narrative: The item is delight (chephets), read as sense 'delight in the law' and typed as affect (101/102): an inclination of feeling, not an act of will. Its bearer is the blessed man of v1 (105), and the operation (106) is the positive counterpart to the three refusals that open the psalm - he does not walk, stand, or sit with the wicked; instead his delight is fixed on the LORD's law, desire relocated to the good. The target is delight itself, the settled object of the affection (107), welded to it by the coupling 'delight-in-law' (112). No source is recorded (103 absent): the psalm does not say what kindled this love, only that it is his. No seat is given (104 none) - the delight is not lodged in a named organ but simply owned by the man; no manner is marked (108 none) - it is delight plainly. Intensity, specifier, effect, and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): the verse states the affection and its object but not its degree, its precise shade, its downstream fruit, or any forbidding of it - the fruit-image of v3 lies outside this row. The discovery (114) fixes the finding: the interior does not merely avoid evil, it positively loves the law, and this affection fuels the day-and-night meditation. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: In this opening psalm the truly happy man is described first by what he refuses - he keeps no company with the mocking and the corrupt - and then, more deeply, by what he loves: God's instruction is his joy. His pleasure has simply moved house, away from evil and onto the good. The poem does not tell us how this love began or where in him it sits; it does not measure how strong it is or spell out what it produces. It only says the love is his, and real, and that it is this delight - not grim duty - that keeps him poring over God's words all day and all night. What the man wants has been quietly retrained toward the right thing.
narratives.variation_note: This reading is delight fixed on God's law as a standing affection of the righteous man; #2 (16:3) turns the same delight toward the godly community, and #3 (111:2) toward God's works studied - the object of the pleasure shifts from law to people to deeds.

narratives.narrative: Here 'good' (tob) is read not as a quality but as a craving after benefit: sense 'the many who crave some good', typed as volition (101/102) - an act of wanting rather than a feeling. The bearer is 'the many' (105), the anonymous crowd of v6, and the operation (106) is their restless question, 'Who will show us any good?' - a diffuse, unanchored reaching for benefit. The target is that very restless-craving (107), bound by the coupling 'who-shows-good' (112). No source is named (103 absent): the crowd's hunger has no stated origin, which is itself telling - it floats free, attached to no object. No seat (104 none): the craving is ascribed to the group as such, not organ-located; no manner (108 none): it is bare wanting. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition all absent (109/110/111/113) - the verse gives the appetite but not its measure or its issue. The discovery (114) draws the governing contrast: the interior of the many is a vague, unanchored hunger for good, set over against the psalmist's own located joy in the light of God's face. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: Around the praying psalmist stands a restless crowd, and their inner life shows in one weary question: who will show us anything good? It is a hunger that reaches out but lands on nothing in particular - a craving for benefit with no address. The poem does not say where this longing comes from or how fierce it is, and it never tells us whether it is ever satisfied; it simply leaves the many wanting. That empty, drifting appetite is set against the psalmist himself, whose own joy has found its home in the light of God's face. The difference is the point: one hunger wanders, the other has come to rest.
narratives.variation_note: This reading takes tob as an aimless craving for 'some good' in the restless crowd; the other tob readings are settled convictions - good found in God alone (16:2), nearness to God as one's good (73:28), one's own good repaid with evil (109:5), the good who receive God's good (125:4), the goodness of brothers in unity (133:1). Here alone 'good' names a hunger rather than a possession.

narratives.narrative: The item is 'straight' (yashar), read as sense 'longing for the straightened way' and typed as volition (101/102) - a wanting, here the desire for a clear path. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is his petition that God lead him in righteousness and make the way straight before him amid his enemies. The target is that desire-for-guidance (107), coupled 'make-way-straight' (112). No source is recorded (103 absent) - the longing arises from his exposed situation, unattributed. No seat (104 none): the desire is not placed in a bodily organ; no manner (108 none): it is asked plainly. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition all absent (109/110/111/113) - the verse voices the want without grading it or reporting its fulfilment. The discovery (114) sharpens it: the interior longs not merely for rescue but for a level, unambiguous path through the enemies' terrain - it wants clarity, not only safety. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: Hemmed in by watching enemies, the psalmist asks God for something more particular than escape: he wants the road ahead made plain and level. His longing is not just to be saved but to see clearly where to walk, to have no ambiguity under his feet while foes surround him. The poem does not explain what stirred this desire or how intense it burns, and it stops before telling us whether the smooth path was granted. It simply shows a man whose deepest wish, under pressure, is for a straight way - he craves guidance as much as rescue.

narratives.narrative: 'Desire' (taavah) here is read as sense 'the afflicted's desire heard' and typed as affect (101/102). The bearer is the afflicted (105) - the crushed and helpless of the psalm - and the operation (106) is that the LORD hears their desire, strengthens their heart, and inclines his ear: the longing of the crushed is answered. The target is that answered-longing (107), coupled 'desire-heard' (112). No source is named (103 absent): the desire wells up from affliction itself, its origin unstated. No seat (104 none): though v17 speaks of the heart being strengthened, the desire-row itself assigns no organ-seat to the desire; no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113) - the verse reports the desire and its hearing but does not grade the longing or detail its result beyond the strengthening named in the operation. The discovery (114) sets the finding against the psalm's other interior: over against the wicked's inner life (who says in his heart 'God has forgotten'), the afflicted's inner longing is the one God bends down to and steadies. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: The psalm has just exposed the inner voice of the oppressor, who tells himself God has forgotten and will never call him to account. Against that, it lifts up the inner life of the crushed and the helpless - and their longing is the one God actually stoops to hear. He listens to their desire, steadies their trembling hearts, and turns his ear toward them. The poem does not say what first kindled this longing or how strong it runs, and it does not spell out every result; it fixes on the single fact that God attends to it. The oppressor's heart talks itself into safety; the sufferer's heart is heard.
narratives.variation_note: This reading is the afflicted's God-heard longing that God answers; #2 (21:2) is the king's heart's-desire granted, and #3 (112:10) is the wicked's desire that perishes unfulfilled - the same word runs from answered longing, to satisfied longing, to frustrated longing depending on whose it is.

narratives.narrative: 'Good' (tob) here is read as sense 'no good apart from you' and typed as cognition (101/102) - not a craving but a confession, an act of the knowing mind. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is his declaration to the LORD that he has no good apart from him: all his welfare is located in God alone. The target is total-dependence (107), coupled 'no-good-apart' (112). No source is recorded (103 absent). No seat (104 none): the confession is not lodged in a named organ; no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114) names the operation as a radical relocation of the good: nothing outside God counts as the self's benefit. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116). The type is worth marking - unlike the crowd's craving-good of 4:6 (volition), this is cognition, a settled judgement rather than a restless want.
narratives.story: The psalmist turns to God and says something total: apart from you I have nothing good. It is not a burst of feeling but a considered conviction - a decision about where his whole welfare lies. Everything he would call good he has relocated onto God alone, so that nothing outside God still counts as benefit to him. The poem does not say what brought him to this settled mind, where in him it rests, or how forcefully he holds it; it simply states the confession. Where an anxious crowd elsewhere merely wonders who will show them any good, this man already knows: only God.
narratives.variation_note: Among the tob readings this one is a reasoned confession that God is the only good (cognition), distinct from the crowd's aimless craving (4:6, volition) and from the later settled reckoning that nearness to God is best (73:28). Here 'good' is a claim about where all benefit is located.

narratives.narrative: 'Delight' (chephets) here is read as sense 'delight in the saints' and typed as affect (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is that the saints in the land, the excellent ones, are those in whom is all his delight - joy taken in godly company. The target is holy-fellowship (107), coupled 'delight-in-saints' (112). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the interior's pleasure is fixed on the godly; its chosen company of joy is selected by holiness - which the very next verse contrasts with the multiplied sorrows of those who run after another god. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: The psalmist tells us where his heart's pleasure goes: to the good and faithful people around him, the ones he calls excellent. They are the company he delights in, and his choice of them is shaped by their holiness. The poem does not explain how this affection arose or how deep it runs; it simply names the object of his joy. And it sets that joy in sharp relief - for the very next breath speaks of those who chase after other gods and only multiply their own griefs. His delight has picked its people.
narratives.variation_note: Same word as 1:2 and 111:2, but here delight rests on the godly community rather than on God's law (1:2) or God's works (111:2) - the affection keeps its shape while its object moves from text, to people, to deeds.

narratives.narrative: 'Lines' (chebel, the measuring-line and so the allotted portion) is read as sense 'a pleasant lot gladly owned' and typed as affect (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is that the boundary lines have fallen for him in pleasant places, and he owns his inheritance as beautiful - contentment with what he has been given. The target is contentment (107), coupled 'pleasant-lines' (112). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114) draws a fine distinction: this is not the same as taking God as one's portion (v5) - it is the glad acceptance of the actual circumstances of one's life, the concrete lot itself received as good. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: Using the picture of a surveyor's cord marking out a plot of land, the psalmist says his measured-out portion has landed in lovely places - and he is glad of it. This is contentment with the actual shape of his life, the very circumstances handed to him, received as beautiful rather than resented. The poem does not say what produced this settled gladness or how strongly he feels it. It is worth noticing this is a slightly different thing from calling God his portion a verse earlier: here he is happy not only with God but with the plain facts of the life God has allotted him.

narratives.narrative: 'Desired' (chamad) is read as sense 'desire the law above gold' and typed as affect (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is that the rules of the LORD are more to be desired than much fine gold and sweeter than honey - a valuing that outbids treasure. The target is supreme-valuing (107), coupled 'desire-above-gold' (112). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113) - notably no intensity marker, though the comparison itself ('than much fine gold') carries the weight the intensity-row leaves blank. The discovery (114) names the operation as appraisal: the interior weighs the word against wealth and prefers it. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: The psalmist does something with God's commands that we usually do only with money: he prices them. Set beside the finest gold, God's rules are worth more to him; set beside honey fresh from the comb, they taste sweeter. His inner life here is an act of weighing and choosing - and the word wins. The poem does not tell us where in him this desire sits or how it first grew, and it puts no number on its strength beyond the comparison itself. But the verdict is clear: given the choice between treasure and truth, he wants the truth more.

narratives.narrative: 'Desire' (taavah) here is read as sense 'the heart's desire granted' and typed as affect (101/102). The bearer is the king (105); the operation (106) is that God has given the king his heart's desire and not withheld the request of his lips - a longing fully met. The target is fulfilled-longing (107), coupled 'desire-not-withheld' (112). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none) - though 'heart's desire' names the heart in the text, the desire-row records no organ-seat - no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the operation is the satisfaction of the inmost want - the interior's deepest wish granted. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: The king had a deepest wish, and God gave it to him - the very thing his heart wanted, the very request his lips made, held back in no part. Here the inner longing is not thwarted or merely heard but wholly satisfied. The poem does not say what the desire was made of, or where it lived in him, or how it burned; it simply reports that it was met, in full and without reservation. It is a portrait of an inner want carried all the way to fulfilment.
narratives.variation_note: Same word (taavah) as 10:17 and 112:10, but here the desire is completely satisfied - the king's wish granted in full - whereas at 10:17 it is the afflicted's desire merely (but graciously) heard, and at 112:10 it is the wicked's desire that comes to nothing. This is the fulfilment pole of the word's range.

narratives.narrative: 'Want' (chaser, to lack) is read as sense 'I shall not want' and typed as affect (101/102) - here the affect of settled sufficiency, the felt absence of craving. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is that because the LORD shepherds him, the self lacks nothing - a contentment that rests in being led and fed. The target is contentment (107), coupled 'shall-not-want' (112). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the operation is settled sufficiency - the interior, under a shepherd, is freed from craving and anxiety about need. Within a family of desire and longing, this reading is a striking inversion: the item is the stilling of desire. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: In a collection of psalms full of hunger and longing, this one names the opposite: I shall not want. Because the LORD is his shepherd, the psalmist's inner life is emptied of craving - no gnawing lack, no anxious reaching for what he needs, because he is being led to pasture and water and simply has enough. The poem does not measure this peace or say exactly how it took hold; it states it as a settled fact of the shepherded life. Where others in these psalms thirst and pant, this heart rests. Being cared for has quieted the appetite.

narratives.narrative: 'Desires' (chaphets) here is read as sense 'who desires life and to see good' and typed as volition (101/102) - an act of wanting. The bearer is the seeker of life (105), the 'what man is there' of v12, and the operation (106) is that the self names the one who desires life and loves many days to see good - the very longing the psalm sets out to answer. The target is that desire-for-life (107), coupled 'desire-life-good' (112). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the operation surfaces a universal want - a good, long life - and then prepares to redirect it, teaching that the way to it runs through the fear of the LORD and a tongue kept from evil. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: The psalm pauses to ask a question everyone quietly answers yes to: is there anyone here who wants a good, long life? It names a desire we all recognise - to live, to see many good days. But rather than simply grant it, the poem turns that universal wanting toward an unexpected road: reverence for God, honest speech, turning from evil and doing good. The poem does not say where this desire lodges in him or how fiercely it burns; it simply lifts up the common human wish and points it somewhere higher. Our ordinary appetite for a good life becomes the hook on which a deeper teaching hangs.

narratives.narrative: 'Delight' (chaphets) here is read as sense 'those who delight in my vindication' and typed as affect (101/102). The bearer is those who favour the right (105); the operation (106) is the psalmist's petition that those who delight in his righteousness shout for joy and be glad, saying 'Great is the LORD' - the joy of those who love justice. The target is shared-vindication-joy (107), coupled 'delight-in-righteousness' (112). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114) invokes a company whose interior is gladdened by the vindication of the right, and folds their delight into God's own: 'Great is the LORD, who delights in the welfare of his servant.' Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: Set against enemies who whisper 'Aha, just what we wanted!' at his downfall, the psalmist calls for a very different company - the people who are actually glad when justice is done. He wants them to break into shouts of joy at his vindication and to cry, 'Great is the LORD.' The poem does not say where this gladness sits in them or how strong it runs; it simply names a whole group whose inner life lights up when the right thing wins. And it quietly links their joy to God's own, for he too delights in his servant's good.
narratives.variation_note: H2655 chaphets appears here (35:27) and at 70:2. Here the delight is clean and shared - people rejoicing over justice done; at 70:2 the very same word turns malicious, enemies who 'delight in my hurt.' The identical inner motion is aimed once at another's vindication and once at another's ruin.

narratives.narrative: 'Feast on' (ravah, to drink one's fill) is read as sense 'they feast on the abundance of your house' and typed as affect (101/102). The bearer is those who take refuge (105); the operation (106) is that the children of men feast on the abundance of God's house and drink from the river of his delights - satisfaction found in God himself. The target is satisfaction-in-God (107), coupled 'feast-on-abundance' (112). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114) draws the contrast that governs the whole psalm: over against the wicked's dry, sleepless scheming in vv1-4, here is an interior that drinks its fill from God - even the word 'delights' (eden) hums under the river-image. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: The psalm has just painted the wicked man lying awake plotting, his inner world all trouble and deceit. Then it turns to the opposite picture: people who shelter under God's wings and simply feast - eating their fill of the richness of his house, drinking from a river of his own delights. Their inner life is one of deep satisfaction, filled up at the source. The poem does not say how strong this contentment is or where it sits in them; it just sets the drinker beside the schemer. One heart is parched and grasping; the other is soaked through with joy.

narratives.narrative: 'Delight' (anag) here is read as sense 'delight yourself in the LORD' and typed as affect (101/102), framed as a command. The bearer is the hearer (105) whom the psalm addresses; the operation (106) is the summons to delight in the LORD, who will then give the desires of the heart - joy in God that reshapes desire itself. The target is delight (107), coupled 'delight-in-the-LORD' (112). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the operation is the cultivation of joy in God; the interior that delights in him finds its wants aligned and met - so this is not a bribe (delight and God will pay out) but a reordering, where delighting in God retunes what the heart even wants. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: Instead of fretting over how well the wicked are doing, the psalm gives a command aimed straight at the inner life: take your delight in the LORD. The promise attached is that he will give you your heart's desires - but the deeper point is that delighting in God quietly retunes those desires, so that what you come to want and what he gives begin to line up. The poem does not say how this joy is stirred up or how deep it must go; it simply issues the instruction. Learn to enjoy God, and your wanting itself is remade.

narratives.narrative: 'Longing' (taavah) here is read as sense 'all my longing is before you' and typed as affect (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist (105), sick, guilt-crushed, abandoned by friends; the operation (106) is that all his longing is before the Lord and his sighing is not hidden from him - the desire laid wholly open to God. The target is open-longing (107), coupled 'longing-before-you' (112). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the operation exposes the interior - the self takes a strange comfort that its whole ache is already visible to God, nothing of the longing needing to be explained or performed. Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: Weighed down by sickness and guilt, deserted by friends and stalked by enemies, the psalmist says something quietly steadying: all my longing lies open before you, and my sighing is no secret to you. He does not have to explain his ache or dress it up; God already sees the whole of it. The poem does not measure how deep this longing goes or say what stirred it; its comfort is simply that nothing of the inner cry is hidden. When everyone else has stood off at a distance, the one relief is that God already knows exactly what he wants and how much he hurts.

narratives.narrative: 'Delight' (chaphets) here is read as sense 'I delight to do your will, your law within my heart' and typed as affect (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is that the self delights to do God's will, its law within its heart - obedience become desire. The target is delighted-obedience (107), coupled 'delight-to-do-will' (112). No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) - though the text says 'your law is within my heart', the delight-row assigns no organ-seat to the delight itself; no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the operation is obedience felt as joy - the law is not an external weight but an internalised delight, set here above the sacrifices God 'has not delighted' in (v6). Role = characteristic (115); locus = internal:ib-state (116).
narratives.story: Over against heaps of sacrifices that never truly pleased God, the psalmist offers something better: not grudging compliance but joy. 'I delight to do your will,' he says, 'your law is within my heart' - obedience that has stopped being a burden and become a pleasure. The poem does not say what kindled this or where exactly it sits; it simply reports that doing God's will is now something he wants, not merely something he must. The law has moved from a rule pressing on him from outside to a delight lodged within.
narratives.variation_note: One of five readings of chaphets-delight. Here delight is in doing God's will (obedience internalised); it turns elsewhere to God's commandments (112:1, 119:35), to God's works and haven (68:30, 107:30), and darkly to war (68:30) and to another's hurt (109:17) - the same delight running from glad obedience to bloodlust depending on its object.

narratives.narrative: 'Pants' (arag) is read as sense 'pant / long' and typed as action (101/102) - not a static state but a straining motion. The bearer is 'my soul' (105, a span-pair with the deer of the simile), and the operation (106) is to pant, to long. The target is 'for you, O God' (107). The manner (108) is the vivid simile, 'as a deer pants for flowing streams' - the desire pictured as a hunted or parched animal straining toward water. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat (104 none) - the longing is ascribed to the whole soul, not to a bodily organ; and the coupling is explicitly none (112) - the panting stands alone, unwelded to any further inner motion. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113) - the verse gives the straining and its object but does not grade it or name its issue. The discovery (114): the soul's desperate thirst-longing for God, the whole self yearning for him as for water in a drought. Notably the locus is external:god (116) - the desire reaches out of the self toward God, not resting inward. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The image is unforgettable: a deer, driven and dry, straining toward running water - and that, the psalmist says, is exactly how his whole self reaches for God. This is not a quiet mood but a desperate motion, a panting toward the one thing that can slake the thirst. The poem does not say what set off this longing or measure how strong it is, and it lets the panting stand entirely on its own, tied to nothing else in him. What it does make plain is the direction: the whole reach is outward, away from himself and toward God, the way a parched animal reaches for a stream.

narratives.narrative: 'Thirsts' (tsame) here is read as sense 'thirst' and typed as action (101/102). The bearer is 'my soul' (105, a span-pair with the soul), and the operation (106) is to thirst. The target is 'for God, the living God' (107). No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) - the thirst belongs to the soul as such; no manner (108 none) - here the thirst is stated plainly, without the desert-simile that colours the parallel at 63:1. The coupling (112) is 'of the soul', binding the thirst to the whole self. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the parching desire for God, thirst turned spiritual, the soul dry for the living God as land is dry for water. Locus is external:god (116) - the craving strains outward toward God. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Right after the panting deer, the psalmist names the craving directly: my soul thirsts for God, for the living God. It is the plain language of a dry throat turned into the language of the spirit - a whole self gone parched for the one who is its water. He even asks aloud, 'when shall I come and appear before God?' The poem does not say what caused this thirst or how fierce it has grown; it simply states it and points it outward, toward the living God. The soul here is not resting in itself but reaching past itself for the only thing that can quench it.
narratives.variation_note: H6770 tsame appears at 42:2 and 63:1, both thirst-for-God. Here (42:2) the thirst is stated bare, coupled simply to the soul; at 63:1 it gains a seat (the soul), a body-pairing (the fainting flesh), and the desert-land simile - the same craving rendered starker and more embodied in the wilderness psalm.

narratives.narrative: 'Pleasing' (tov) here is read as sense 'good / pleasing - a goodly theme' and typed as status (101/102): not an act but a quality resting on a thing. The bearer is 'the theme' that fills the heart (105). Strikingly, the operation is none (106) and the target is none (107) - and these silences are the finding: this row is a state, not a movement. The good does not act on anything or reach toward a goal; it simply is the excellence of the subject. What is present is the coupling (112): the good is the very theme the heart overflows with, span-paired to the overflowing heart. No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none), no intensity/specifier/effect/prohibition (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the goodly matter that stirs the heart to song - the excellence of the king as subject that moves the poet's heart to overflow. Locus is internal:ib-state (116) - the good lodged as an inner condition of the heart. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The wedding song opens with a heart that cannot hold still: 'my heart overflows with a good theme.' Here the goodness is not something the poet does but something his subject simply has - the sheer excellence of the king he is about to praise, so fine that it sets his heart running over like a fountain. Nothing is being aimed at or acted upon; the good just sits there, glorious, and the overflow follows. The poem does not say where this goodness comes from or how great it is; it only shows a heart brimming because its subject is so worth singing. The excellence of the theme becomes the pressure behind the song.

narratives.narrative: 'Desire' (avah) here is read as sense 'desire / long for - your beauty' and typed as action (101/102). The bearer is the king (105); the operation (106) is to desire. The target is the bride's beauty (107). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The coupling (112) is span-paired to the bride's self-forgetting - 'the king will desire your beauty' answers her leaving her people and her father's house. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the king's longing for the bride, the strong desire that answers her self-forgetting, the mutual drawing of the royal marriage. This is a rare frankly conjugal desire in the Psalter, and the reading does not spiritualise it away. Locus is internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Turning to the bride, the song tells her plainly what will happen when she leaves her old home behind: the king will desire her beauty. It is a straightforward picture of marital longing - his wanting rising to meet her willingness to forget her people and belong to him. The poem does not explain what stirs this desire or how strong it is; it simply names the mutual pull of the wedding, her self-giving answered by his wanting. The psalm lets this ordinary human desire stand as it is, unhidden, at the heart of a royal marriage.

narratives.narrative: 'Destruction' (havvah, engulfing ruin or greed) here is read as sense 'destruction / engulfing ruin' and typed as status (101/102) - a quality of what the tyrant produces. The bearer is the tyrant, or rather what he plots (105); the operation (106) is 'plotted' - his tongue devises this ruin. The target is none (107): the destruction is not yet aimed at a named victim in this row - it is the ruinous aim itself, sharp as a razor. No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The coupling (112) reaches forward across the psalm: this is the ruin he plots in v2, span-paired to the ruin he strengthens himself in at v7 - the same word closing a circle. The discovery (114): the engulfing ruin the tyrant devises with his tongue. Locus is internal:ib-state (116) - the destructiveness is an inner disposition, seated in the plotting self. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The psalm turns on a violent man whose weapon is his tongue. What his mouth is busy devising is sheer ruin - a plotted, engulfing destruction, sharp as a razor. Here the evil is not yet landing on a victim; it is the ruinous intent itself, the appetite for wreckage that fills the schemer. The poem does not say where this destructiveness comes from or how strong it burns; it simply shows it as the man's own inner bent. And it quietly plants a hook: the very ruin he is plotting here will come back, later in the psalm, as the ground he ends up standing on.
narratives.variation_note: Both readings of havvah are in Psalm 52 and are deliberately linked. In v2 the destruction is what the tyrant plots (his tongue's ruinous aim); in v7 it is what he takes refuge in (the ruin become his ground and undoing). The same word marks first the crime and then the self-inflicted punishment - the difference is the whole arc of the psalm.

narratives.narrative: 'Destruction' (havvah, engulfing greed and ruin) here is read as sense 'destruction / engulfing greed - his destruction' and typed as status (101/102). The bearer is the tyrant (105); the operation (106) is 'took refuge in' - he made his ruin his stronghold, trusting the abundance of his riches and seeking safety in his own destruction. The target is none (107): the ruin is not aimed outward now but has curled back onto him. No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The coupling (112) is the same havvah his tongue plotted at v2, span-paired back to it. The discovery (114): the ruin the tyrant made his refuge, closing the circle - the destruction his tongue plotted becomes the ground he stands on, and so his undoing. Locus is internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: By the end of the psalm the violent man's ruin has come home to him. He would not make God his refuge; instead he trusted his piled-up riches and took shelter in the very destructiveness that defined him. The greed he lived by becomes the ground he stands on - and it gives way beneath him. The poem does not measure this ruin or trace where it began; it simply lets the circle close. The engulfing destruction his tongue once plotted against others turns out to be the thing he leaned on, and it swallows him.
narratives.variation_note: This is the second and closing havvah of Psalm 52. Where v2 named the ruin as the tyrant's outward plot, v7 turns it inward and terminal: the same destruction becomes his own refuge and his fall. The shift from what he aims at others to what he rests in himself is the point.

narratives.narrative: 'Fly away' (uph) is read as sense 'fly away' and typed as action (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist in his longing (105); the operation (106) is to long to fly away, to escape. The target (107) is span-paired: 'to be at rest, far from the turmoil.' The manner (108) is 'like a dove with wings' - the wish clothed in the image of a bird's flight. No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none). The coupling (112) is span-paired to the longing to be at rest - flight and rest bound together as one wish. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the overwhelmed soul's yearning to escape - the wish for flight from unbearable turmoil, the instinct to flee rather than face the betrayal, longing for distance from the storm of the city. This is desire read honestly as avoidance, not aspiration. Locus is internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Crushed by violence in the city and, worse, by the betrayal of a close friend, the psalmist blurts out a very human wish: oh, for wings like a dove - I would fly away and be at rest. His longing here is not noble aspiration but the simple ache to escape, to get far from a storm he cannot bear to face. Flight and rest are one thing in his mind: to be gone is to be at peace. The poem does not say how strong this urge is or where it comes from beyond the turmoil around him. It lets the honest impulse stand - the desire, under unbearable pressure, simply to be somewhere else.

narratives.narrative: 'Ruin' (havvah, engulfing destruction) here is read as sense 'ruin / engulfing destruction - ruin in its midst' and typed as status (101/102). The bearer is the city's wicked (105); the operation is none (106) and the target is none (107) - and that double silence is the finding: this ruin does not act or aim, it simply sits. It is a condition lodged at the city's heart, not a deed done to a victim. The manner (108) is 'in its midst' - the destruction enthroned at the centre. The coupling (112) span-pairs it to the oppression and fraud that never depart the marketplace. No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): engulfing destruction at the city's heart, the devouring destructiveness from which oppression and fraud never depart. Locus is internal:ib-state (116) - though it fills a city, the reading treats it as an inner condition of the wicked who make the city what it is. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Looking out over a city torn by violence, the psalmist sees ruin sitting right at its heart - not an act being committed at one moment, but a settled state of destructiveness lodged in the middle of things, with oppression and fraud circling it and never leaving. It is destruction as an atmosphere, the inner corruption of the wicked spread through the whole place. The poem does not say where it came from or how bad it will get; it simply shows it enthroned at the centre. The city's very heart has become the home of ruin.

narratives.narrative: 'Tramples' (shaaph, to pant after and so to crush) here is read as sense 'trample / pant after - man tramples on me' and typed as action (101/102). The bearer is man, the enemies (105); the operation (106) is to trample, to hound. The target (107) is the psalmist. The manner (108) is 'all the day long' - a relentless, unresting pursuit. No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none). The coupling (112) span-pairs the trampling to the oppression of the attacker. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the relentless hounding that drives the plea - the enemies' eager pursuit, 'all day long,' the pressure that meets its answer in the psalmist's trust of v3. Notably the locus is external:person (116): this desire is aimed out of the self at another - an appetite to crush - not an inward state. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: This psalm shows desire in its predatory form. The psalmist's enemies do not merely oppose him; they pant after him, trampling him down all day long, hounding him without a pause. Their inner drive is an appetite to crush - a wanting pointed straight at another person's harm. The poem does not say what feeds this hunger or how far it will go; it simply names the relentless, all-day pressure of it. And it sets that pressure up for its answer: against the tramplers' craving to destroy him, the psalmist puts his trust in God.
narratives.variation_note: H7602 shaaph is read at 56:1 and 57:3, both of enemies who hound the psalmist. Here (56:1) the trampling is present and relentless - 'all day long' - with no mention of its end; at 57:3 the very same hounding is named together with its reversal, the God who will 'put to shame him who tramples.' This reading holds the pressure; the next holds the overthrow.

narratives.narrative: 'Tramples' (shaaph) here is read as sense 'trample / pant after - him who tramples on me' and typed as action (101/102). Unlike its parallel at 56:1, this row carries a source (103, present): the trampler is defined as the one 'whom God will put to shame' - his hounding is already framed by its coming overthrow. The bearer is the enemy (105); the operation (106) is to trample, to hound; the target (107) is the psalmist. The manner is none (108) and the coupling is none (112) - the enemy's aggression is stated more bleanly here, stripped of the 'all day long' colouring and left standing under God's verdict. No seat (104 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the hounding foe (same verb as Ps 56) whom God will shame - the trampler overthrown by the God who is exalted above the heavens. Locus is external:person (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Again an enemy pants after the psalmist to crush him - but this time the hounding is named in the same breath as its undoing. God, the psalmist says, will put to shame the very one who tramples on him. The predatory desire is still there, still aimed at another's ruin, but here it stands already under sentence, its overthrow announced before it can finish its work. The poem does not dwell on how fierce or how long the pursuit is; it leans instead on the reversal. The trampler's appetite meets a God exalted above the heavens who will shame it.
narratives.variation_note: The companion to 56:1. The distinguishing mark is the source: at 57:3 the trampler is expressly 'whom God will put to shame,' his aggression framed by its defeat, and the manner/coupling of relentlessness drop away. Where 56:1 holds the raw pressure of the hounding, 57:3 holds its overthrow - the same craving to crush, read once as threat and once as already-judged.

narratives.narrative: 'Take pleasure' (ratsah, to delight in or approve) here is read as sense 'take pleasure / delight - they take pleasure in falsehood' and typed as action (101/102). The bearer is the enemies (105); the operation (106) is to take pleasure, to delight. The target (107) is span-paired: 'in falsehood.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The coupling (112) span-pairs the pleasure to the falsehood they love. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the heart's delight in lies - not merely using falsehood but loving it, the inner corruption behind the hypocrisy that follows, where they bless with their mouths but inwardly curse. Locus is internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The psalm exposes something darker than mere dishonesty: these enemies do not just tell lies, they enjoy them. Falsehood gives them pleasure; they relish deceit. Their inner delight has fastened onto the wrong thing entirely, so that lying is not a tool they use reluctantly but a thing they love - which is why they can bless with their mouths while cursing underneath. The poem does not say how deep this corruption runs or where it began; it simply names the appetite. Pleasure itself has gone rotten in them, taking its joy in the lie.

narratives.narrative: 'Thirsts' (tsame) here is read as sense 'thirst - my soul thirsts for you' and typed as status (101/102) - the parched condition itself. Unlike the bare thirst of 42:2, this row records a seat (104, present): the soul, span-paired - the thirst is expressly lodged in the nephesh. The bearer is the psalmist, his soul (105); the operation (106) is to thirst for; the target (107) is God. The manner (108) is 'as in a dry and weary land without water' - the desert-simile absent at 42:2 but present here. The coupling (112) span-pairs the soul's thirst to the flesh fainting for God, so soul and body strain together. No source (103 absent). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): spiritual longing felt as bodily thirst, the soul's craving for God as parching as desert thirst - God alone the water that slakes it. Locus external:god (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Alone in the wilderness of Judah, in a dry and weary land where there is no water, the psalmist finds the desert an exact picture of his own inside: my soul thirsts for you, my flesh faints for you. The craving is lodged deep in him and it pulls his whole body along with it - soul and flesh together straining toward God as parched ground strains toward rain. The poem does not measure this thirst or say what first opened it up; it simply lets the desert speak for the man. God alone is the water, and everything in him is dry for it.
narratives.variation_note: The starker of the two tsame readings. At 42:2 the thirst is stated bare and simply coupled to the soul; here at 63:1 it is seated in the soul, paired with the fainting flesh, and framed by the desert-land simile - the same craving rendered more embodied and more desperate in the wilderness setting.

narratives.narrative: 'Delight' (chaphets) here is read as sense 'delight / take pleasure - who delight in war' and typed as status (101/102). This row carries a source (103, present): the war-lovers are defined as those 'whom God rebukes and scatters,' their pleasure framed by its judgement. The bearer is 'the peoples' (105); the operation (106) is to delight, to take pleasure; the target (107) is 'in war,' span-paired. No seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The coupling (112) span-pairs them as the war-loving peoples God scatters. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the bloodlust of hostile nations - the peoples who love war, whom God rebukes and scatters, a warlike relish that God's judgement ends so that kings may bring him tribute instead. This is delight read at its darkest - pleasure taken in slaughter. Locus internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The same inner motion that elsewhere loves God's law here loves bloodshed. The psalm asks God to scatter the peoples who delight in war - nations whose pleasure is fixed on violence, who relish the fight. It is desire gone savage, joy that feeds on battle. The poem does not say how deep this bloodlust runs or where it was born; it names it plainly and sets it under God's rebuke, to be scattered so that kings might come bringing tribute instead. Read without flinching, this is the human capacity to take genuine pleasure in war - and to have that pleasure judged.
narratives.variation_note: One of five chaphets-delight readings, and the darkest alongside 109:17 and 70:2. Here delight is fixed on war itself; elsewhere the same word loves God's will (40:8), God's commandments (112:1, 119:35), and the longed-for haven (107:30). The identical inner pleasure runs from glad obedience to a relish for slaughter, marked out by its object.

narratives.narrative: 'Zeal' (qinah) here is read as sense 'zeal / jealousy - zeal for your house has consumed me' and typed as status (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is that the zeal has consumed him, span-paired - it devours the one who holds it. The target (107) is 'for God's house.' The manner (108) is 'consuming, all-devouring,' span-paired - the zeal named by the very way it burns. The coupling (112) span-pairs it to the reproaches of God's revilers falling on him. No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113) - yet the operation and manner together do the work an intensity-row would: this is desire so total it eats the man. The discovery (114): burning devotion to God's honour that devours the psalmist, passion for God's glory so total it becomes his suffering, drawing the revilers' reproach onto himself. Locus external:god (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Here longing burns so hot it becomes self-destructive. The psalmist's zeal for God's house - his fierce love for God's honour - has eaten him up, consumed him from the inside. It is passion at its most extreme, a devotion so total that it becomes his affliction, so that the insults hurled at God land squarely on him. The poem does not need to grade how strong this is; it says the zeal is devouring him. This is desire pointed at God's glory and running to the very edge of self-consumption - love for God's house that costs the man himself.
narratives.variation_note: H7068 qinah is read at 69:9 and 119:139, both zeal for God consuming the psalmist. Here (69:9) the zeal is for God's house and draws the revilers' reproach onto him; at 119:139 it is zeal for God's word, kindled by foes who forget it. The same all-consuming fire, aimed once at the temple's honour and once at the honour of Scripture.

narratives.narrative: 'Delight' (chaphets) here is read as sense 'delight / take pleasure - who delight in my hurt' and typed as status (101/102). The bearer is the enemies (105); the operation (106) is to delight, to take pleasure; the target (107) span-pairs 'in the psalmist's hurt.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The coupling (112) span-pairs them to those who seek his life. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): malicious pleasure in another's harm - the enemies' relish for the psalmist's ruin, a delight twisted to feed on suffering, the exact opposite of those who delight in God. Locus internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The psalmist's enemies have an appetite for his pain: they delight in his hurt, taking real pleasure in the prospect of his downfall. It is joy turned inside out - a capacity for delight that has fastened onto someone else's suffering as its food. The poem does not say how far this malice reaches or what bred it; it simply names the twisted pleasure and asks that it be turned back in shame. Set beside those who delight in God, this is the same inner motion gone rotten: gladness that lives off another's ruin.
narratives.variation_note: H2655 chaphets appears at 35:27 and here (70:2). At 35:27 the delight is clean - people glad at justice done and at God's care for his servant; here it is malicious - enemies glad at the psalmist's hurt. The identical inner pleasure is aimed once at another's vindication and once at another's ruin, and the contrast is the finding.

narratives.narrative: 'Envious' (qana) here is read as sense 'be envious / jealous - I was envious of the arrogant' and typed as status (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist (105) himself - the confession is his own; the operation (106) is to be envious. The target (107) span-pairs 'the arrogant / the wicked's prosperity.' The manner (108) is 'seeing the prosperity of the wicked' - the envy triggered by sight. The coupling (112) span-pairs it to the envy that almost made him stumble (v2). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the root of the near-fall is envy - the jealousy stirred by the ease of the godless, the corrosive resentment a believer can feel watching the wicked flourish, the very disease the psalm diagnoses and cures. Locus internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The psalmist makes an uncomfortable confession about his own heart: watching the wicked prosper, fat and untroubled, he grew envious of them. His feet nearly slipped - not through any outward sin but through this inward resentment, this jealous ache at seeing the godless do so well. The poem does not measure how deep the envy went or excuse it; it names it honestly as the disease that almost brought him down. This is desire in its sour form, the longing to have what the arrogant have - and the rest of the psalm is the slow cure of exactly this sickness.

narratives.narrative: 'Desire' (chaphets) here is read as sense 'desire / delight - nothing on earth that I desire besides you' and typed as status (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is to desire, to delight in; the target (107) is God alone, nothing besides. The manner (108) is the cry 'whom have I in heaven but you?' The coupling (112) span-pairs the desire to God who holds, guides, and receives him (vv23-24). No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the summit of the psalm - God alone the object of desire, the envy of v3 utterly cured and replaced by a longing for nothing but God himself. Locus internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: This is where the psalm's long struggle finally lands. The man who once envied the wicked their prosperity now says: whom have I in heaven but you? and there is nothing on earth I desire besides you. Every rival want has fallen away; his whole desire has narrowed to God alone. The poem does not say how strong this longing is - it does not need to, for it has emptied out every other object. The sour envy of the opening has been completely healed and replaced by a single, clean desire: God himself, and nothing else, held fast by the God who holds him.

narratives.narrative: 'Good' (tob) here is read as sense 'good - it is good to be near God' and typed as status (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is to reckon good, to find best, span-paired. The target (107) span-pairs 'to be near God.' The manner (108) span-pairs 'having made the Lord GOD his refuge.' The coupling (112) span-pairs it to making God his refuge and telling his works. No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the psalmist's settled conclusion, answering the psalm's opening 'God is good' (v1) - his own reckoning that nearness to God is the true good, not the wicked's prosperity but communion with God, the crisis fully resolved. Locus external:god (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The psalm that opened by insisting 'God is good' now closes with the man's own hard-won verdict: for me, it is good to be near God. After all the envy of the prosperous wicked, he has reckoned up what is truly best and named it - not their wealth, but nearness to God, having made the Lord his refuge. The poem does not measure this conviction; it states it as a conclusion reached, the whole crisis resolved. What began as a general truth about God has become a personal settlement of the heart: the good he wants is simply to be close to God.
narratives.variation_note: Among the tob readings this is a settled reckoning that nearness to God is best (status/disposition), the resolved twin of the aimless craving at 4:6 and the confession at 16:2. Here 'good' is neither hunger nor bare claim but a verdict reached at the end of a struggle - what a man concludes is truly worth wanting.

narratives.narrative: 'Craved' (nephesh, the appetite of the soul) here is read as sense 'crave' and typed as disposition (101/102) - a standing bent of appetite. The bearer is 'they' (105), the wilderness generation; the operation (106) is to crave, to lust after; the target (107) is food. No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The coupling (112) binds the craving to the testing heart - 'they tested God in their heart by demanding the food they craved.' Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the soul-appetite that drove the wilderness rebellion. This reading names desire as the engine of unbelief - the craving that puts God to the test. Locus internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Asaph retells the wilderness story as a story about appetite. The people craved food - a deep soul-hunger - and that craving became rebellion: they used it to test God, demanding he prove himself by spreading a table in the desert. The poem does not say how strong the hunger was or where it came from; it shows how it worked, hardening into unbelief. Here desire is not innocent need but the very engine of distrust: a craving that, instead of trusting the God who had already struck water from the rock, dared him to deliver.

narratives.narrative: 'Craved' (taavah) here is read as sense 'crave' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is 'they' (105); the operation (106) is to crave; the target (107) is the food. No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The coupling (112) binds the craving to the fullness - 'he gave them what they craved,' and they ate and were well filled. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the desire God met, the lust indulged unto judgement. The disturbing note is that this craving is satisfied - God grants it - and the granting is itself the beginning of the disaster. Locus internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: This time the craving gets exactly what it wanted. God gave the people the food they craved, and they ate and were stuffed full. But the granting is no mercy here - it is the setup for judgement. The poem does not measure the hunger; it shows it fed to the brim, an indulged appetite that carries its own doom inside it. This is the unsettling truth the psalm presses: sometimes the worst thing that can happen to a craving is to have it granted. Desire satisfied on its own terms becomes the road to ruin.
narratives.variation_note: The two taavah readings in Psalm 78 are a matched pair marking two moments of the same craving. At v29 the craving is satisfied - fed to fullness; at v30 it is unslaked when wrath strikes, the food still in their mouths. Together they frame the appetite between its granting and its punishment: filled at v29, cut off mid-craving at v30.

narratives.narrative: 'Craved' (taavah) here is read as sense 'craving / lust' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is 'they' (105); the operation (106) is to lust; the target (107) is 'after food.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The coupling (112) binds the craving to the wrath that fell mid-meal - 'before they had satisfied their craving, while the food was still in their mouths,' the anger of God rose. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the unslaked lust when wrath struck. Here the same appetite of v29 is caught at the opposite moment - not filled but interrupted, judgement falling before the craving could be exhausted. Locus internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: A single verse later the craving is shown from its far side. They had not yet had their fill - the food was still in their mouths - when God's anger rose and struck down the strongest of them. The appetite that was being fed at one moment is cut off at the next, judgement arriving mid-bite. The poem does not grade the lust; it freezes it at the instant of its interruption. Where the previous line showed a craving stuffed full, this one shows the same craving caught unsatisfied, the eating and the wrath collapsing into one terrible moment.
narratives.variation_note: The companion to v29. Where v29 holds the craving satisfied (fed to fullness), v30 holds it unslaked - interrupted by wrath while the food is still in their mouths. The same lust is read once as granted and once as cut short, the pair together making the appetite the hinge of the judgement.

narratives.narrative: 'Fatherless' (yathom) here is read as sense 'fatherless' and typed as status (101/102) - a condition, not an act. The bearer is the fatherless (105); the operation (106) is to lack a defender; the target (107) is 'before the court.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The coupling (112) pairs the fatherless with the weak. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the orphan without protector, the classic object of justice denied. This item sits at the family's edge - not a desire but a state of helpless need, the vulnerability that just claims call the gods to answer. Locus internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: In God's courtroom charge against unjust rulers, the fatherless child stands as the test case. The orphan is the one with no defender - the classic figure of need, whose rights the powerful can trample precisely because there is no father to speak for him. The poem does not dramatise the child's feelings; it names the bare condition of being without protection before the court. This is need in its most defenceless form, and the whole indictment turns on it: real justice is measured by whether the one who has no one is given his due.
narratives.variation_note: H3490 yathom is read at 82:3 and 109:9. Here (82:3) the fatherless is the object of justice God demands - the vulnerable whom rulers must defend; at 109:9 the same word appears in a curse, the psalmist asking that his enemy's children be made fatherless. The one word names the orphan first as the protected of God's justice and then as the target of imprecation.

narratives.narrative: 'Better' (tob) here is read as sense 'better' and typed as disposition (101/102) - a settled inclination that prefers one thing over another. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is to value, to prefer; the target (107) is 'a day in God's courts.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The coupling (112) pairs it with choosing the threshold - he would rather be a doorkeeper in God's house than dwell in the tents of wickedness. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the reckoning of devotion, God's presence weighed against every alternative and found worth more - a day in the courts against a thousand elsewhere. Locus internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The pilgrim does the arithmetic of love: one day in God's courts is worth more to him than a thousand days anywhere else. He would rather stand at the threshold of God's house as a mere doorkeeper than live comfortably among the wicked. His inner life here is an act of weighing and preferring, and God's presence outweighs every rival. The poem does not say how the preference arose or how strong it is beyond the comparison itself. It simply shows a heart that has counted the cost and decided: nearness to God, even at its humblest, beats every other prize.

narratives.narrative: 'Longs' (kasaph) here is read as sense 'long' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is the pilgrim (105); the operation (106) is to long, to yearn; the target (107) is 'for God's courts.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The coupling (112) pairs the longing with the fainting soul - 'my soul longs, yes, faints for the courts of the LORD.' Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113) - yet the paired 'faints' carries the intensity the marked row leaves blank. The discovery (114): the ache of desire for God's dwelling, longing so strong it exhausts. Locus internal:ib-state (116). Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: How lovely is God's dwelling place, the pilgrim cries - and his longing for it is so strong it wears him out. His soul does not merely wish for the temple courts; it yearns and faints for them, aching with desire to be where God is. The poem does not need to measure this longing, because it shows it exhausting the man who feels it. Even the sparrow finding a nest by the altar stirs his envy. This is homesickness for God's presence, a desire so intense that the wanting itself leaves him spent.

narratives.narrative: 'Pleasing' (arab) here is read as sense 'pleasing' and typed as state (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist's meditation (105) - his inner musing is what is to be pleasing. The operation (106) is to be pleasing, acceptable; the target (107) is God. No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The dimensions here run slightly transposed: the coupling is recorded as 'external:god' (112) and the locus as 'paired with the meditation' (116) - together they fix the movement as the inner meditation directed Godward, seeking his acceptance. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the acceptability sought for the inner worship, that the musing may delight God. This is desire turned reflexive - the longing that one's own longing and thought would please God. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: As the psalm sings of God's vast works, the poet makes a quiet wish about his own inner life: may my meditation be pleasing to him. He wants the very musing of his mind - his private turning-over of God's greatness - to be acceptable, even delightful, to God. The poem does not say how strong this wish is or where it sits; it simply voices the hope. It is a gentle, reflexive kind of desire: not craving something from God, but longing that his own thoughts about God would themselves bring God joy.

narratives.narrative: 'Pleasure' (nephesh, here the will or discretion) is read as sense 'pleasure / will' and typed as faculty (101/102) - notably not an affect or craving but a faculty of the self, the capacity to decide. The bearer is Joseph (105); the operation (106) is to exercise his will; the target (107) is 'binding princes at his pleasure.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The dimensions run transposed here: the coupling is recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112) and the locus 'paired with his affliction and his teaching' (116) - the once-fettered slave's discretion set against his former chains. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): Joseph's own will and discretion, the authority given the once-fettered slave, now free to bind princes as he sees fit. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Here the word usually rendered as craving or soul is used for something else: Joseph's own free will. Once a prisoner in irons, he is now raised to rule Egypt and may bind its princes 'at his pleasure' - by his own discretion, as he sees fit. This is not appetite but authority: the capacity to decide, handed to the man who had been a fettered slave. The poem does not dwell on his feelings; it marks the reversal. The one who had no say over his own body now governs princes at his will, his affliction turned into command.

narratives.narrative: 'Craving' (avah) here is read as sense 'craving' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is 'the fathers' (105), the wilderness generation; the operation (106) is to crave; the target (107) is 'food in the desert.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The dimensions run transposed: coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with the wanton desire' (116) - this craving (avah) sits alongside its twin, the wanton lust (taavah) named in the same verse. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the lusting after food, the greed that tested God. Locus/role: role = characteristic (115). This reading must be held distinct from the wanton-desire of the same verse - the difference between them is itself a finding.
narratives.story: Retelling the wilderness rebellion, the psalm says the people fell into craving out in the desert - a hungry reaching for food that quickly curdled into a test of God. The poem does not measure the craving or trace its root; it simply names the greedy wanting that drove them to put God on trial in the wilderness. This craving is deliberately paired with a second word in the same line, a 'wanton' desire, so that one verse holds two faces of the same appetite. Here the stress falls on the plain wanting itself: hunger that would not trust, and demanded instead.

narratives.narrative: 'Wanton' (taavah) here is read as sense 'wanton' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is 'the fathers' (105); the operation (106) is to have a wanton craving; the target (107) is 'in the wilderness.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The dimensions run transposed: coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with the craving and the testing' (116) - this wanton lust stands beside the craving (avah) of the same verse and the testing of God that follows. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the fierce appetite that ruled them, desire become idolatry. Where the paired 'craving' names the wanting, this word names its wildness - the lust that had become a master. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The same verse that speaks of the people's craving deepens it with a second, sharper word: their desire was wanton - a wild, ungoverned appetite that had taken them over. It is craving grown into something like idolatry, a lust that ruled them and dared to test God in the desert. The poem does not grade this hunger; it colours it, marking not just that they wanted but how fiercely and recklessly they wanted. Held beside the plainer craving of the same line, this word supplies the wildness: an appetite that had stopped serving them and started mastering them.

narratives.narrative: 'Jealous' (qana) here is read as sense 'jealous / envy' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is 'men in the camp' (105) - Korah's company; the operation (106) is to be jealous; the target (107) is 'of Moses and Aaron.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). The dimensions run transposed: coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with the earth swallowing the rebels' (116) - the envy set against its judgement, the ground opening to swallow them. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the envy of Korah's company against God's chosen leaders. Here jealousy is not against a rival's wealth but against another's God-given office - resentment of appointed leadership. Locus: role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The wilderness catalogue of sins turns to a jealousy aimed at leadership: men in the camp grew envious of Moses and Aaron, God's chosen. Their resentment was not for riches but for another's God-given place - a grudging anger that these men, and not they, had been appointed. The poem does not measure the envy; it names it and lets its end speak, for the ground opened and swallowed the rebels. This is desire as resentment of office, the refusal to accept another's calling - and it is shown running straight into judgement.

narratives.narrative: 'Thirsty' (tsame) here is read as sense 'thirsty' and typed as state (101/102) - a bodily condition. The bearer is the wanderers (105), lost in desert wastes; the operation (106) is to be thirsty; the target (107) is 'in the desert.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with hunger' (116) - thirst set beside hunger as the two edges of the wanderers' need. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the parched wanderers, thirst added to hunger. This is desire as sheer bodily lack - need at its most basic, the emptied self about to faint. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The psalm's first portrait is of people lost in a trackless desert, finding no city to live in - and hungry and thirsty, their very life fainting inside them. Thirst here is not a metaphor but a plain bodily emptiness, the raw lack of a body running dry. The poem does not measure it or explain it beyond the wasteland they wander; it simply lets the need press until they cry out. This is desire stripped to its most basic form: a parched body reaching for water, the emptiness that finally drives them to call on the LORD.

narratives.narrative: 'Hungry' (raeb) here is read as sense 'hungry' and typed as state (101/102). The bearer is the wanderers (105); the operation (106) is to be hungry; the target (107) is 'in the desert.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with thirst and the fainting soul' (116). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the starving wanderers, need pressing on the body - 'hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them.' Hunger here is the plain condition of lack that will find its answer only when God fills it. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Alongside their thirst, the lost wanderers are hungry - starving as they stumble through the waste, their strength failing until the life nearly goes out of them. The poem does not dress this up; it is the body's simple, desperate need for food. It does not say how long they had gone without or how they came to be there; it just presses the hunger until they cry to the LORD in their trouble. This is appetite in its barest form - an empty stomach in an empty land - and the psalm holds it there, waiting to show how God answers it.
narratives.variation_note: H7457 raeb runs three times through Psalm 107. Here (v5) hunger is raw need in the desert, part of the wanderers' fainting; at v9 it is the hungry soul God fills with good things; at v36 it is the hungry given a settled home. The same word tracks from bare lack, to lack satisfied, to lack turned into belonging.

narratives.narrative: 'Hungry' (raeb) here is read as sense 'hungry' and typed as state (101/102). The bearer is 'the hungry soul' (105); the operation (106) is to be hungry; the target (107) is 'then filled.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with the hungry soul filled' (116). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the starving self God feeds - 'the hungry soul he fills with good things.' Here the same hunger of v5 is caught at the moment of its answer, need turned to satisfaction. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: A few lines on, the psalm turns the hunger toward its resolution: he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things. The same emptiness that had them fainting in the desert is now met and filled to the full by God. The poem does not measure the hunger; it shows it answered, need becoming plenty. This is the hinge of the psalm's refrain - that the God who is cried to in trouble is the God who fills the empty. The appetite is not scolded here but satisfied, the starving soul heaped with good.
narratives.variation_note: The satisfied face of the psalm's hunger. At v5 the hunger is raw lack in the desert; here at v9 the very same hungry soul is filled with good things by God. Where v5 shows the need, v9 shows its answer - the word moving from emptiness to fullness.

narratives.narrative: 'Longing' (shaqaq) here is read as sense 'longing' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is 'the longing soul' (105); the operation (106) is to long; the target (107) is 'for satisfaction.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with the soul satisfied' (116). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the yearning self God fills, desire met with good - 'for he satisfies the longing soul.' Set beside the bodily hunger of the same verse, this word names the inner reaching itself, the appetite as such that God answers. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The same verse that speaks of the hungry being filled names the inner side of that need: God satisfies the longing soul. Here the stress falls not on an empty stomach but on the reaching itself - the soul's yearning, its appetite for fulfilment, which God meets and fills. The poem does not measure this longing or say where it began; it simply pairs the wanting with its answer. It is a small but real distinction from the plain hunger beside it: this word is the desire, and the good news is that the God who is cried to fills exactly that desire with good.

narratives.narrative: 'Desired' (chaphets) here is read as sense 'desire' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is the sailors (105), tossed on the storm; the operation (106) is to long for; the target (107) is 'their haven.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with the gladness' (116) - the longed-for harbour set beside their gladness when the waters grew quiet. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the longed-for harbour, the goal of the storm-tossed. This is desire as the pull toward a place of safety - the sailors' whole want fixed on the harbour God finally brings them to. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The sailors' portrait ends in a longing fulfilled. Battered by a storm that made their courage melt, they cried out, and God stilled the waves - and then brought them to the very haven they had desired. Their whole want, through the terror, had been fixed on that safe harbour. The poem does not measure the longing; it simply follows it to its glad arrival, the desired port reached at last. Here desire is the homeward pull of people in danger, and the psalm shows God answering it by bringing them exactly where they longed to be.

narratives.narrative: 'Hungry' (raeb) here is read as sense 'hungry' and typed as status (101/102). The bearer is 'the hungry' (105); the operation (106) is to be hungry; the target (107) is 'then given a home.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with being settled in a city' (116). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113).
