The discovery (114): the needy God settles, hunger answered with a home - 'there he lets the hungry dwell.' Here the raw hunger of v5 has become the occasion of settled belonging: God gives the hungry not just a meal but a place to live. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: In the psalm's final scene the hungry are not merely fed but housed. God lets the hungry settle down, planting them in a city to live in, where they sow fields, plant vineyards, and multiply. The bare need that opened the psalm has become the ground of a whole settled life. The poem does not measure the hunger; it shows it answered generously, lack turned into home and harvest. This is the fullest reach of the psalm's refrain: the God who fills the empty stomach also gives the empty-handed a place to belong.
narratives.variation_note: The third and most expansive raeb reading. At v5 hunger is desperate lack; at v9 it is filled with good things; here at v36 it becomes settled belonging - the hungry given a home, a city, fields. The word travels from need, to satisfaction, to a whole established life.

narratives.narrative: 'Good' (tob) here is read as sense 'good' and typed as disposition (101/102) - but here the good is the psalmist's own conduct. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is to do good; the target (107) is 'to his enemies.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with the evil returned' (116). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the psalmist's good, met with evil - 'they reward me evil for good, and hatred for my love.' Here 'good' names the wronged man's own kindness, thrown back at him as hatred - the grievance that fuels the psalm's terrible curses. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Before the psalm erupts into its ferocious curses, it states the wound behind them: the psalmist did good, gave love, prayed for his accusers - and got evil and hatred in return. Here 'good' is his own kindness, met with betrayal. The poem does not measure it; it simply lays down the injustice, love repaid with hostility, as the ground of everything that follows. This is the ache that the rest of the psalm turns, uncomfortably, into imprecation: a man whose genuine good was answered with evil, and who now pours out his outrage.
narratives.variation_note: Among the tob readings this one is unusual: 'good' is the psalmist's own conduct toward others (kindness given), not a benefit desired or a quality of God. Set beside the aimless craving (4:6), the confession (16:2), and the settled verdict (73:28), here 'good' is what he does and has thrown back at him - good repaid with evil.

narratives.narrative: 'Fatherless' (yathom) here is read as sense 'fatherless' and typed as status (101/102). The bearer is 'the enemy's children' (105); the operation (106) is to be fatherless; the target (107) is 'by his death.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with the widow and the curse' (116). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the imprecation reaching the enemy's children, bereaved by his fall - 'may his children be fatherless.' Here the orphan is not the protected of God's justice but the object of a curse, the psalmist asking that his foe's children be made fatherless. Read without softening, this is a hard prayer. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: In the thick of his curses the psalmist wishes on his enemy the very thing God elsewhere defends against: may his children be fatherless and his wife a widow. The orphan, who in another psalm is the one God's justice protects, is here the target of a bitter prayer - the enemy's downfall reaching all the way to his bereaved children. The poem does not flinch from this; it lets the imprecation stand. It is one of the harshest turns in the Psalter, and reading it honestly means seeing that the same word for the defenceless can also be spoken as a curse.
narratives.variation_note: H3490 yathom read twice, in mirror image. At 82:3 the fatherless is whom God's justice defends - the protected vulnerable; here at 109:9 the same word is a curse, the psalmist asking that his enemy's children be made fatherless. The one condition is spoken first as the object of divine mercy and then as the aim of human imprecation.

narratives.narrative: 'Delight' (chaphets, negated) here is read as sense 'delight' and typed as disposition (101/102), but the row is a negation - the operation (106) is 'not delight.' The bearer is the enemy (105); the target (107) is 'in blessing.' The finding here is an absence within the interior itself: the man did not delight in blessing, so the delight-that-should-be is missing. No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with loving to curse' (116) - the missing delight in blessing set against a positive love of cursing. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the enemy's aversion to blessing, blessing now kept far from him - 'he did not delight in blessing; may it be far from him.' The judgement fits the interior: a man who took no pleasure in blessing is left without it. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The psalm reads the enemy's inner life by what is missing from it: he loved to curse, and took no delight at all in blessing. Where a healthy heart would find pleasure in blessing others, his simply did not - the delight was absent, and cursing filled the empty place. The poem does not measure this; it names the void and pronounces its fitting sentence: since he found no joy in blessing, let blessing stay far from him. Here the finding is a silence inside a man - a pleasure that should have been there and was not - and the curse simply hands him the emptiness he chose.
narratives.variation_note: One of five chaphets-delight readings, and the only one framed as a negation. Elsewhere the delight is present and fixed - on God's will (40:8), commandments (112:1, 119:35), the haven (107:30); here it is the delight that is absent, a man who does not delight in blessing. The missing pleasure is as much a finding as any present one.

narratives.narrative: 'Delight' (chephets) here is read as sense 'delight' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is 'those who study' (105); the operation (106) is to delight; the target (107) is 'in God's works.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'external:god' (112), locus 'paired with studying them' (116) - the delight bound to the studying it drives. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the pleasure in God's works that drives the study, love that seeks to know - 'great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them.' Here delight is generative: it does not merely rest but sets the mind searching. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The psalm praises God's great works and then tells us who really looks into them: those who delight in them. Here pleasure and study run together - it is the ones who love God's works who pore over them, their delight becoming the engine of their searching. The poem does not measure this joy or say where it began; it simply ties it to the studying it produces. This is delight that will not sit still: a love for what God has done that keeps sending the mind back to examine, to understand, to know more.
narratives.variation_note: The third chephets reading. At 1:2 the delight is in God's law, at 16:3 in the godly community; here at 111:2 it is in God's works, and the mark of it is that the delight drives study - love that wants to know. The same pleasure keeps moving its object from text, to people, to deeds.

narratives.narrative: 'Delight' (chaphets) here is read as sense 'delight' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is 'the man' (105) who fears the LORD; the operation (106) is to greatly delight - the intensity built into the operation itself; the target (107) is 'in God's commandments.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'external:god' (112), locus 'paired with the fear of the LORD' (116) - delight in the commandments joined to the fear of God as the two marks of the blessed man. Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent as marked rows (109/110/111/113), though 'greatly' in the operation carries the degree. The discovery (114): the joy in God's law that marks the God-fearer, obedience loved not merely obeyed. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The blessed man of this psalm is known by two things held together: he fears the LORD, and he greatly delights in his commandments. His obedience is not grudging; it is joyful, a real pleasure taken in God's law. The poem pairs this delight with reverence, so that awe and joy are not opposites but partners in the same heart. It does not say where the delight came from; it marks its strength - 'greatly' - and lets it define the man. Here is desire pointed at God's word: not fear that merely obeys, but a heart that loves what it is commanded.
narratives.variation_note: The fourth of the chaphets-delight readings. Here delight is in God's commandments, joined to the fear of the LORD and marked 'greatly'; elsewhere it is delight in God's will (40:8), in the haven (107:30), and darkly in war (68:30) or another's hurt is its cousin word. The intensity here ('greatly') is unusual among the readings, matching the God-fearer's whole-hearted love.

narratives.narrative: 'Desire' (taavah) here is read as sense 'desire' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is 'the wicked man' (105); the operation (106) is to have his desire perish; the target (107) is 'unfulfilled.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'internal:ib-state' (112), locus 'paired with the wicked's melting away' (116). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): the craving of the wicked come to nothing, appetite frustrated forever - 'the desire of the wicked will perish.' Here desire is read at its terminal point: not answered, not merely delayed, but extinguished with the man who held it. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: The psalm's final line pronounces the fate of the wicked man's wanting: his desire will perish. Watching the righteous flourish, he gnashes his teeth and melts away - and everything he craved dies with him, unfulfilled forever. The poem does not measure this desire; it simply announces its end. Here appetite is shown at its bleakest: a wanting that reaches out and is granted nothing, snuffed out along with the man. Set against the God-fearer who delights in the commandments, the wicked man is defined by a craving that comes, in the end, to absolutely nothing.
narratives.variation_note: The third taavah-desire reading, and the terminal one. At 10:17 the afflicted's desire is heard; at 21:2 the king's is granted in full; here at 112:10 the wicked's desire perishes unfulfilled. The same word marks longing answered, longing satisfied, and longing extinguished - sorted entirely by whose desire it is.

narratives.narrative: 'Delight' (sus/shaashua, to rejoice) here is read as sense 'delight' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is to delight, to rejoice; the target (107) is 'in God's law.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'paired with the whole DELIGHT-arc of the psalm' (112), locus 'external:god' (116). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): delight in the testimonies weighed against all wealth - 'in the way of your testimonies I delight as much as in all riches.' The comparison does the pricing an intensity-row would: God's word set level with all riches and loved as much. Role = characteristic (115).
narratives.story: Deep in the great psalm about God's law, the psalmist measures his joy against money: I delight in the way of your testimonies as much as in all riches. His pleasure in God's word is set on the same scale as wealth - and it holds its own. The poem does not say where this delight came from or grade it beyond that comparison; it simply weighs the word against riches and finds it as dear. This is one note in a long song of delight running through the whole psalm: a heart that treasures God's instructions the way others treasure gold.

narratives.narrative: 'Delight' (shaashua) here is read as sense 'delight' and typed as disposition (101/102). The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation (106) is to delight, to rejoice; the target (107) is 'in God's law.' No source (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner (108 none). Coupling recorded 'paired with the whole DELIGHT-arc of the psalm' (112), locus 'external:god' (116). Intensity, specifier, effect, prohibition absent (109/110/111/113). The discovery (114): delight vowed, paired with not forgetting - 'I will delight in your statutes; I will not forget your word.' Here delight is bound to memory: the resolve to enjoy the law and the resolve to keep it in mind are one act. Joy and memory are tied together - to take pleasure in God's law is also to hold on to it. The poem does not say what kindled this delight or how strong it is; it simply vows it. And it comes back through the psalm: the same delight is what lets him speak of God's law before kings without shame, and what sets him apart from enemies whose hearts have grown fat and unfeeling. His pleasure in the word is a steady, chosen thing.

God's words are both the thing he loves and the thing that advises him. The poem does not measure this delight; it simply shows how much it carries. And across the psalm it proves to be life itself: had God's law not been his delight, he says, his affliction would have destroyed him; in trouble and anguish, the commandments remain his joy. This is delight that doubles as a lifeline - pleasure in the word that keeps a man alive.

His love for God's way is not passive; it becomes the very argument for asking God to keep him walking there. The poem does not say how the delight arose or how deep it runs; it simply lets it drive the request. This is one more note in the psalm's long music of delight - a heart that so enjoys God's path that its natural prayer is to be led further down it.

His desire for God's commands is offered almost as proof of his sincerity, and it flows straight into a plea for life - because I long for them, revive me. The poem does not measure this longing or say where it began; it simply holds it up and lets it become a prayer. And it returns near the psalm's end, where his longing for God's salvation stands beside his delight in God's law. Wanting the word and wanting to live have become, for him, the same reach.

narratives.story: The psalmist's longing has reached the point of collapse: my soul faints for your salvation. He does not merely want rescue; the wanting has worn him out, drained him, left him spent with waiting. The poem marks this as a state he is in rather than a neat reach toward a goal - the longing itself has become exhausting. It does not measure how long he has waited or where the ache sits; it simply shows a soul fainting under the strain of hope deferred, holding on to God's word even as its strength gives out.

Worn out from looking - straining toward a comfort that has not yet come - his very eyes give out, and he can only ask, when will you comfort me? The poem does not measure the wait; it lets the exhausted eyes speak for it, and the same weariness returns later as he watches for God's salvation. This is desire located in the act of looking itself: eyes that ache from searching the horizon for a God who seems slow to come.

He opens his mouth and pants, he says, because he longs for them. The desire is the cause; the gasping is its effect. The poem does not measure the longing or say where it came from; it simply shows it breaking out of him, too strong to stay quiet. This is wanting that cannot be hidden - a craving for God's word that makes a man gasp for it the way a runner gasps for air.

Like someone gasping in thirst, he opens wide - a gesture of pure craving, aimed at nothing in particular except to take in what he desires. The poem does not say how strong this is beyond the image itself; the open mouth says it. Here wanting has become physical, visible - a man so hungry for God's commandments that his very mouth falls open in longing for them. It is desire you could see, not just feel.

narratives.story: The psalmist pants - breathless with wanting - for God's commandments. It is a striking picture: the same kind of panting that elsewhere describes enemies crushing him underfoot here describes his own breathless craving for God's word. The poem does not measure this or explain it; it simply shows a man out of breath with longing. The very energy that in a foe becomes a hunger to destroy becomes, in him, a hunger for God's commands. He gasps for the word the way a hunted thing gasps - only what he chases is the law he loves.

narratives.story: The psalmist is eaten up by a burning zeal - and what kindles it is that his enemies forget God's words. Their neglect of the law inflames him to the point of being consumed, his passion for God's word turned into an inner fire that wears him down. The poem does not measure this zeal; it says plainly that it is devouring him. Here longing has become fierce, almost painful: not a gentle affection for Scripture but a consuming distress that others treat it as nothing. His love for the word burns hot enough to hurt.

narratives.story: This short pilgrim psalm prays that God's goodness would find the good: do good, LORD, to those who are good, to the upright in heart. Here 'good' is not a craving or a benefit but a quality of the inner person - a settled uprightness of heart. The poem does not say how such goodness arises or measure it; it simply names it and asks that God's own good come to rest on it. Set against those who turn aside to crooked ways, the good are those whose hearts are straight - and the prayer is that like should meet like, God's goodness reaching the good.

narratives.story: Behold, how good it is when brothers live together in unity, the psalm exclaims. Here 'good' names the sheer rightness and worth of people dwelling in harmony - the moral excellence of a shared life without division. The poem does not explain how such unity comes about or measure it; it simply holds it up and calls it good, then likens it to precious oil running down and to the dew of Hermon. This goodness is paired in the same breath with a second word for its sweetness - so that unity is named both as right and as lovely, two sides of one blessing.

Unity is not only right; it is sweet, a delight to live in, and the psalm reaches for images of pleasure to say so: fragrant oil running down Aaron's beard, the fresh dew of Hermon settling on the hills. The poem does not measure this pleasantness or say where it comes from; it simply savours it. Held beside the word 'good,' this one adds the taste to the truth: living together in harmony is not just the right thing but a genuinely lovely thing.

narratives.story: The psalmist prays against the very wanting of his enemies: do not grant the desires of the wicked. Their inner appetite, he sees, is for triumph - to have their schemes succeed and themselves lifted high over the righteous they hunt. The poem does not measure this craving or trace its root; it names it as a will bent on prevailing, and asks God to refuse it. Here desire is read from the outside and prayed against: an appetite for victory over the innocent, so dangerous that the one hope is for God to leave it forever unfulfilled.
